s: Aurora Innovation DEF 14A filed 2 Apr 2026 (holdings as of 23 Mar 2026); AUR close 6.24 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 577,652 Class A plus 37,059,994 Class B shares = 37,637,646 x 6.24 = 235M; age 45 in Aurora S-4 of 15 Jul 2021
did: Co-founded Aurora Innovation in 2017 with Chris Urmson and Sterling Anderson and is its chief scientist, keeping his Carnegie Mellon robotics professorship in Pittsburgh; he built the machine-learning core of the Aurora Driver after running perception and autonomy for Uber ATG.
why: Aurora sold the driver as a subscription to freight carriers rather than building trucks, so Paccar and Volvo carried the vehicle cost while Aurora kept the software margin; founder Class B stock with ten votes meant three engineers retained control through a SPAC listing and three dilutive raises.
obst: Aurora shares fell about 90 percent after the 2021 SPAC listing and crosstown rival Argo AI was shut down by Ford and Volkswagen in October 2022, forcing Aurora to raise capital at depressed prices while burning about 700M a year.
turn: The December 2020 deal to absorb Uber ATG, which handed Aurora 1,200 engineers and a 400M Uber investment without cash leaving the balance sheet.

s: PNC Financial DEF 14A filed 11 Mar 2026 (ownership as of 30 Jan 2026); PNC close 243.13 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 611,417 shares and units x 243.13 = 149M, plus 3.95M deferred compensation balance and 10.9M pension present value disclosed in the same proxy; age 63 printed in proxy
did: Left JPMorgan structured finance in 2002 to become PNC chief financial officer, took over as chief executive in 2013, and turned a Pittsburgh regional bank into the sixth largest US bank by buying National City in 2008 and BBVA USA for 11.6B in 2021.
why: PNC held a 22 percent stake in BlackRock from the 1995 sale of its own asset manager; selling it in May 2020 for 14.4B gave Demchak acquisition currency at the exact moment BBVA wanted out of the US, so he bought a 100B-asset franchise in Texas and the southwest with a windfall rather than with dilution.
obst: He integrated National City in December 2008 while it was failing and PNC was inside TARP, absorbing a bank nearly PNC size with a loan book full of Florida and Ohio mortgage losses.
turn: The May 2020 sale of PNC entire BlackRock stake at the top of the market, converting a passive holding into the BBVA USA purchase.

s: Wesco International DEF 14A filed 17 Apr 2026; WCC close 349.14 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 753,914 shares beneficially owned including 296,637 exercisable options and SARs; the 457,277 shares held outright are worth 160M, options add on top; age 64 printed in proxy
did: Joined Pittsburgh electrical distributor Wesco as operating chief in 2004, became chief executive in 2009, and in June 2020 closed the 4.5B purchase of Anixter International after outbidding Clayton Dubilier and Rice, roughly doubling revenue to about 17B and adding data centre and security wiring.
why: Distribution is a scale and working-capital business: buying Anixter gave Wesco supplier rebate tiers and branch density that smaller rivals cannot match, and the debt taken on to win it was repaid out of the datacentre and grid construction boom that followed, turning leverage into an eightfold share price move.
obst: He became chief executive in 2009 as non-residential construction collapsed and Wesco revenue fell about 25 percent, then took on 4.5B of acquisition debt in June 2020 as covid shut down job sites.
turn: Winning the January 2020 bidding war for Anixter against a private equity buyer that had already signed a deal.

s: MSA Safety DEF 14A filed 26 Mar 2026 (5 percent holder table); MSA close 189.43 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,021,586 shares beneficially owned, 906,108 with sole power and 1,115,478 shared as co-trustee or by spouse, x 189.43 = 383M; age 76 in the April 2020 MSA proxy
did: Third-generation head of MSA Safety in Cranberry Township, joined 1969 and ran it as chief executive from 1991 to 2008, converting a coal-mine equipment maker founded by his grandfather in 1914 into a global maker of firefighter breathing apparatus, gas detection instruments and fall protection.
why: Safety equipment is sold on approval standards, not price: MSA wrote itself into NFPA and MSHA specifications, so every US fire department buying self-contained breathing apparatus had to qualify against a product line MSA already dominated, and replacement cycles rather than new construction drove revenue.
obst: US coal employment collapsed through the 1990s, taking MSA original market with it, while the company carried thousands of product liability claims from miners over coal dust respirators that ran for decades.
turn: The 1990s pivot into firefighter self-contained breathing apparatus, which after the 2001 attacks became a federally funded replacement market.

s: Intuit DEF 14A filed 23 Nov 2022 (931,454 shares beneficially owned) and Intuit Form 4 of 4 Oct 2021 (407,121 shares held outright); INTU close 367.00 on 21 Aug 2026
m: Last outright holding 407,121 x 367 = 149M; full 2022 beneficial figure including exercisable options x 367 = 342M gross; midpoint taken net of option strikes and unobserved sales since he left Intuit board; age 62 printed in JPMorgan 2026 proxy
did: Ran Intuit as chief executive from 2008 to 2018 and as executive chairman to 2022, moving QuickBooks and TurboTax from boxed desktop licences to cloud subscriptions; since 2022 he has been president of Marshall University in Huntington West Virginia, where he lives and files his SEC ownership reports.
why: Small-business accounting has switching costs measured in years of ledger history, so moving that base to a monthly subscription converted a lumpy upgrade cycle into recurring revenue and let Intuit attach payroll, payments and lending to the same file, multiplying revenue per customer without new acquisition cost.
obst: He had to cannibalise the desktop licence business that was Intuit profit engine, and in 2016 sold Quicken, Demandforce and QuickBase to force the company onto QuickBooks Online and TurboTax alone.
turn: The 2013 cloud-first decision and the 2016 divestitures that left Intuit with two subscription products instead of a portfolio.

s: Coherent Corp Form 4 filed 15 May 2024 by Vincent D. Mattera Jr (664,684 shares held directly); COHR close 289.52 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 664,684 shares x 289.52 = 192M; excludes options and any sales after he left Section 16 reporting on retirement in mid 2024; age 67 as of 31 Aug 2023 per Coherent proxy
did: Ran II-VI of Saxonburg Pennsylvania as chief executive from 2014 to June 2024, buying Finisar for 3.2B in 2019 and Coherent Inc for about 7B in 2022, then taking the Coherent name; the combined company supplies the optical transceivers and lasers behind AI datacentre interconnect.
why: II-VI already grew its own crystals and substrates, so buying the transceiver and laser businesses in front of it captured the whole optical chain from selenide and silicon carbide boules to finished modules, which is why AI datacentre demand in 2025 and 2026 landed on a cost base nobody could undercut.
obst: Winning Coherent Inc in a 2021 auction against Lumentum and MKS required roughly 5B of new debt and Bain preferred equity, and the share price then fell about 60 percent through 2022 and 2023 before AI optics demand arrived.
turn: The March 2021 decision to keep raising the bid for Coherent Inc after Lumentum had a signed agreement.

s: Coherent Corp Form 4 filed 16 Nov 2022 by Francis J. Kramer (272,685 direct, 35,000 in a GRAT, 285,401 in a spousal trust, 65,324 options at 19.37); COHR close 289.52 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 593,086 shares x 289.52 = 172M plus option intrinsic value of about 18M; no Section 16 visibility since he left the board in 2022, so sales may have reduced it; age 72 in the II-VI 2021 proxy
did: Joined II-VI in Saxonburg in 1983, was its president from 1985 to 2007 and chief executive from 2007 to 2014, turning a niche maker of infrared optics for carbon dioxide cutting lasers into a vertically integrated photonics manufacturer with plants across China, Singapore, the Philippines and Vietnam.
why: II-VI grew its own crystal materials, so it could enter any market where the optic was the hard part; owning the furnaces meant rivals buying merchant substrates could not match its cost or lead times, and the Asian plants he built won volume telecom work US optics firms could not price.
obst: The company depended on industrial laser cutting optics, a cycle that fell with machine-tool orders in 2001 and again in 2009, and he had to fund diversification out of a small revenue base without diluting the founders.
turn: The January 2010 purchase of Photop Technologies in China, which put II-VI into optical communications components and set up the Finisar deal a decade later.

s: Wabtec DEF 14A filed 31 Mar 2026 (605,402 shares as of 31 Jan 2026); WAB close 297.57 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 605,402 shares x 297.57 = 180M; age 75 printed in the same proxy, which also records his retirement from the board in May 2026
did: Ran Wabtec, the Wilmerding Pennsylvania air-brake maker, as chief executive from February 2006 to May 2014 and then as executive chairman and chairman, buying Faiveley Transport in 2016 and merging in GE Transportation in 2019 to create the largest freight locomotive and rail equipment builder outside China.
why: Air brakes and control systems are safety-certified and effectively single-sourced for the life of a locomotive, so Wabtec earns a high-margin aftermarket annuity on an installed base it keeps enlarging by acquisition; buying GE Transportation added the locomotive itself and the parts stream behind it.
obst: North American rail capital spending collapsed with coal volumes in 2015 and 2016, cutting freight orders sharply just as Wabtec was integrating Faiveley and carrying the debt for it.
turn: The February 2019 completion of the 11B GE Transportation combination, which doubled Wabtec and made the aftermarket the profit engine.

s: CNX Resources DEF 14A filed 26 Mar 2026 (2,781,352 shares, 1.96 percent, as of 9 Mar 2026); CNX close 36.36 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 2,781,352 shares x 36.36 = 101M, including options exercisable within 60 days; age 57 printed in the same proxy
did: Joined CONSOL Energy as an engineer in 1990, ran CNX Gas from 2005, became chief executive of CONSOL in 2014 and split the company in November 2017, keeping the Marcellus and Utica gas business as CNX Resources and spinning off the coal mines; he retired as chief executive on 31 December 2025.
why: CNX owns its Appalachian acreage in fee alongside legacy coalbed methane rights, so it drills without leasing costs and hedges years forward; running a deliberately small, buyback-heavy company instead of chasing volume meant share count fell by roughly a third while gas prices swung.
obst: Henry Hub gas fell under 1.60 in 2020 and Appalachian producers were shut out of ESG-constrained capital, while the 2017 separation left CNX carrying legacy coal-era pension and reclamation obligations.
turn: The November 2017 separation of coal from gas, which repriced the gas business on its own reserves rather than on coal liabilities.

s: EQT DFAN14A filed 13 Feb 2019 by Toby Z. Rice and Derek A. Rice; Rice Energy DEF 14A of 17 Apr 2017; EQT close 53.72 on 21 Aug 2026
m: 272,651 EQT shares held directly and indirectly = 14.6M, plus a beneficiary share of the Rice Energy 2016 Irrevocable Trust holding 5,676,000 EQT shares (305M) split among the Rice brothers, plus Rice Investment Group carry; age 32 as of April 2017 per Rice Energy proxy
did: Co-founded Rice Energy with his father and brothers in 2007 and ran exploration and geology as executive vice president, assembling the Marcellus and Utica position in Greene and Washington counties that EQT bought in November 2017 for about 6.7B; now a partner at Rice Investment Group in Canonsburg.
why: The brothers drilled longer laterals than anyone in southwestern Pennsylvania and owned the midstream that moved their own gas, so they captured the gathering margin as well as the wellhead one; that made the acreage worth more to EQT as a contiguous block than the sum of its wells.
obst: Appalachian gas fell below 1.50 per million BTU in 2015 and 2016, forcing the family to take Rice Midstream Partners public to fund drilling, and after selling to EQT they had to run a 2019 proxy fight to unseat the board of the company that had bought them.
turn: The November 2017 sale of Rice Energy to EQT for cash and stock, followed by the July 2019 proxy win that put his brother Toby in charge of the buyer.
